claims.text: The starting material is a homogeneous CoCrFeNi matrix without self-lubricating phases or secondary microstructures.
Introducing a self-lubricating second phase into CoCrFeNi will promote in situ formation of a lubricious surface layer during sliding.
The resulting surface film will remain stable from room temperature to 800 °C.
A well-dispersed self-lubricating phase facilitates formation of a continuous lubricious oxide or another low-shear surface film.
Under tribological load, the self-lubricating phase reacts with ambient oxygen or undergoes a phase transformation.
The reaction or transformation produces a stable, low-shear film.
The low-shear film minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
Minimizing direct metal contact reduces friction and wear.
At lower temperatures, the introduced phase acts as a barrier to abrasive contacts.
At higher temperatures, the in situ generated lubricious film remains effective.
The modified alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The modified alloy will have a lower wear rate than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The friction and wear improvements will persist under variable loads in ambient air.
Sufficient environmental oxygen is required for the proposed film-forming mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes performance across the full temperature range to in situ formation of a stable lubricious film, whereas the mechanism assigns lower-temperature performance to the second phase acting as an abrasive-contact barrier and does not establish that the film forms or remains stable at low temperature.

The mechanism permits either oxygen-driven reaction or a phase transformation, but the boundary states that sufficient oxygen is required, leaving the oxygen-independent phase-transformation pathway inconsistent with the stated environmental requirement.
